deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of an expert opinion (Gutachten) on the actuarial balance of a widows' pension fund ('Anstalt', 'Casse', 'Direction', 'Interessenten'). It is almost certainly the Göttingen Professoren-Witwen- und Waisenkasse, which Gauss had valued earlier. The page contains no mathematics proper, only actuarial bookkeeping and a methodological critique.

(1) Riemann judges that the Direction's calculation follows correct principles. It would allow a sound judgement of the fund's position if it were carried out more exactly and rested everywhere on correct assumptions.

(2) The Direction found an annual surplus of 3954 Thlr, equivalent to a capital of 98850 Thlr. Implicit step (mine): capitalisation as a perpetuity at 4% interest, so capital = annual amount / 0.04 = 25 × annual amount. Check: 3954 × 25 = 98850.

(3) Riemann's claim: under a sharper calculation this surplus could easily become a deficit of several hundred thousand Thlr.

(4) The main error he has found so far concerns the gain to the fund from unmarried members, especially those under 45. They pay contributions but, while unmarried, create no widow's-pension liability. The Direction valued this gain assuming every unmarried member stays unmarried for life. In fact each marriage turns the gain into a liability.

(5) Data: from an average over the years '185 2/9' (most likely 1852–1859), 66 unmarried persons under 45 join each year. Their average entry age is 30 in one draft and 33 in the final draft. The value of the resulting gain is computed as 12,788,682 (in the Direction's units, 'Nummern').
- A struck subtraction reads 12,788,682 − 12,024,838 = 763,844. This is probably the contributions minus the remaining part.
- The unmarried current members are valued at a capital of 163,589 Thlr, or 6543.56 Thlr per year. Again 4%: 163589 × 0.04 = 6543.56.
- A marginal addition gives 150900 + 12689 = 163589. These are presumably two components of the gain, e.g. present members plus future entrants, or two age classes.

(6) Final draft argument: the life-long-celibacy assumption can hardly be granted even for half of the unmarried under 45 with average age 33. The necessary 'reduction' of this item alone would turn the Direction's surplus into a deficit.
- Implicit (mine): losing even half of the 163,589 gain (≈81,800) and adding the widow liabilities created by those who marry plausibly exceeds the 98,850 surplus.
- Whether other items, recomputed more sharply, would offset or enlarge this deficit cannot be judged from the data available to him.

The next page's logarithmic computations (base-10 logs such as 9.19350, 8.58939) presumably belong to the same actuarial calculations.
errors: Draft inconsistency, not an error: the average age of unmarried entrants is 30 in the struck/earlier passage and 33 in the final passage. These may refer to different groups (entrants vs. present members).

The claim that the needed reduction 'would already turn the surplus into a deficit' is asserted, not derived on the page. It holds only if the loss exceeds 98,850 Thlr. Half of 163,589 is 81,794.5, so the claim relies on the additional widow liabilities created by marriage. This is plausible but not computed here.
The ratio between 12,788,682 ('Nummern') and the capital value 163,589 Thlr is not explained on the page. The units are unclear.

results.what: Capitalisation of annual surplus/gain as a perpetuity at 4% (factor 25) in valuing a widows' fund
results.modern_name: Present value of a perpetuity; actuarial valuation of a pension fund
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th century actuarial practice (cf. Gauss's valuation of the Göttingen widows' fund, 1845–51)

results.what: Critique that the gain from unmarried members was overstated by assuming life-long celibacy; marriage probabilities must enter the valuation
results.modern_name: Multiple-decrement / marital-status transition modelling in widows' pension actuarial valuation
results.usually_credited_to: Actuarial science of widows' funds (Tetens, Gauss and others); Riemann's involvement with the Göttingen Witwenkasse is known in the biographical literature

deep.surprise_reason: Routine actuarial bookkeeping and a sensible methodological critique in a report on a widows' fund. Riemann's involvement in the evaluation of the Göttingen professors' widows' fund (after Gauss) is known, so this is a minor biographical detail rather than new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Annual surplus 3954 Thlr capitalised at 4% gives 98850 Thlr
Capital 163589 Thlr at 4% equals 6543.56 Thlr per year
Marginal addition of the two components of the unmarried-members gain
Half the gain alone (81794.5) is less than the surplus, so the deficit claim requires additional marriage liabilities

transcription_corrections: '185 2/9' is most likely Riemann's shorthand for the period 1852–1859 (average over those years), not a fraction.
'12.788,682' and '12788,682' should be read as the integer 12,788,682 (the struck subtraction 12,024,838 / 763,844 confirms the digit grouping), not as a decimal.
'würde {+einen Überschlag[?]+} ein sicheres Urtheil' is better read as an interlinear 'einen Überschlag' inserted above 'ein sicheres Urtheil' (alternative wording).
'Veranschlagt[?] worden ist' belongs to the struck draft ('...von den Unverheiratheten unter 45 Jahren zu ... veranschlagt worden ist').
'[-Er-] {+Erheblich+}' is better read as the insertion 'Erheblich' modifying 'Die Reduction' ('Die erhebliche Reduction...'), with a struck word replaced.
Marginal figures 150 900 / 12 689 / 163,589 form a separate addition column in the left margin, not part of the running text.
